derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], $M=\mathbb R\times\Sigma$ is the Cartesian product equipped with the smooth product structure of [F3], hence is a smooth four-manifold. The tensor $g=-N^2 dx^0\otimes dx^0+h$ is smooth and symmetric. At each $(x^0,y)$ the tangent space splits as $\mathbb R\partial_{x^0}\oplus T_y\Sigma$, and for $a\in\mathbb R$ and $v\in T_y\Sigma$ its quadratic form is $-N(y)^2a^2+h_y(v,v)$. Since $N(y)>0$ and $h_y$ is positive definite by [F4], this form has one negative direction and three positive directions, and its direct-sum matrix is nondegenerate; hence it has signature $(-,+,+,+)$ by [F5].

The field $\partial_{x^0}$ is smooth and has squared norm $-N^2<0$, so it is future timelike for the selected time orientation. Its local flow translates $x^0$ and fixes $y\in\Sigma$; since $N$ and $h$ are independent of $x^0$, this flow pulls $g$ back to itself and hence $\mathcal L_{\partial_{x^0}}g=0$ by [F6]. Thus the field is Killing, and its lapse equals the prescribed $N$ by [A3] and $N>0$.

By [F7], $dV_h$ is a globally defined positive smooth density with associated Borel measure $\operatorname{vol}_h$. This measure is finite on compact $\Sigma$, and the notation $\int_\Sigma f\,dV_h$ denotes its integral for Borel $f$. The profiles $T=T_0/N$ and $\mu=(\mu_0-q\Phi)/N$ are smooth because $N$ is smooth and strictly positive. Their length-coordinate conventions follow from [A1], while $q\Phi$ has energy units by [A2]. The measure construction and integration use the stated $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ premise [F11].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]).

For a nonnegative Borel $f:M\to[0,\infty]$ and any chart partition $(x_i,\varphi_i)$,
$$\int_M f\,d\mu_r=\sum_i\int_{x_i(U_i)}(\varphi_i f r)_{x_i}\,d\lambda_n,$$
with values in $[0,\infty]$ and all zero-times-infinity products equal to zero. For positive smooth $r$ and compactly supported smooth real $f$, this equals the smooth density integral $\int_Mfr$. For real or complex $f\in L^1(\mu_r)$ the same chart formula holds, interpreted by real and imaginary positive and negative parts; the series converges absolutely. On the completion, nonnegative measurable functions and real or complex $L^1$ functions have Borel representatives modulo completed null sets, and the formulas are applied to those representatives.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Choose a nondegenerate bounded closed interval $I_0\subset U$ whose interior contains $\mu_0$. It is compact by [F5], so $I_0\times\Sigma$ is compact by [F5]. Define $G(r,x)=(T_0/N(x),(r-q\Phi(x))/N(x))$. This map is continuous and takes values in $D$, so its image $K\subset D$ is compact by [F6]. With the Euclidean subspace metric, K is a compact metric space. Since $p\in C^2(D)$, $p_\mu$ and $p_{\mu\mu}$ are continuous and bounded on $K$ by [F11], and uniformly continuous there by [F7]. Also $N$ attains a minimum $N_{\min}>0$ on compact $\Sigma$ by [F11]. For $r\in I_0$ put $f(r,x)=N(x)p(G(r,x))/(k_BT_0)$. For sufficiently small $h$ with $r+h\in I_0$, the mean value theorem [F8] gives a point $r_h(x)$ between $r$ and $r+h$ with $(f(r+h,x)-f(r,x))/h=\partial_r f(r_h(x),x)$. The profiles satisfy $|G(r_h(x),x)-G(r,x)|\le |h|/N_{\min}$ uniformly in $x$, so uniform continuity of $p_\mu$ makes these quotients converge uniformly to $\partial_r f(r,x)=p_\mu(G(r,x))/(k_BT_0)$ by [F10]. By [F4] and finite total volume [F2], the difference between the integrals is bounded by $\operatorname{vol}_h(\Sigma)\sup_x|(f(r+h,x)-f(r,x))/h-\partial_r f(r,x)|$, which tends to zero. Hence differentiation passes through the finite-volume integral and yields $\partial_{\mu_0}W_{\rm hs}=\int_\Sigma p_\mu/(k_BT_0)\,dV_h$.

Differentiating $\partial_r f=p_\mu(G)/(k_BT_0)$ by [F10] gives $\partial_r^2 f=p_{\mu\mu}(G)/(N k_BT_0)$. The same mean value argument, now using uniform continuity of $p_{\mu\mu}$ on $K$ and $1/N\le1/N_{\min}$, shows that the difference quotients of $\partial_r f$ converge uniformly in $x$ to $\partial_r^2 f$. Applying the density-integral estimate from [F4] therefore gives $\partial_{\mu_0}^2W_{\rm hs}=\int_\Sigma p_{\mu\mu}/(N k_BT_0)\,dV_h$.

By [A1], each integrand value in the second formula is nonnegative because $N(x)>0$, $k_B>0$ by [A3], and $T_0>0$. By [F3] the Riemannian density is positive, and [F4] makes its integral nonnegative; hence $\chi_{\rm hs}\ge0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty compact smooth three-manifold without boundary, let $h$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, and give $\mathbb R$ its usual topology and the standard smooth structure generated by the global identity chart $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R}:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Give $M=\mathbb R\times\Sigma$ the canonical product smooth structure. Write $x^0=ct_{\rm phys}$ for the standard length coordinate on $\mathbb R$ and use spatial coordinates measured in metres. For a smooth function $N:\Sigma\to(0,\infty)$, extend $N$ constantly along $\mathbb R$ and define the metric on $M$ by $g=-N^2\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+h$, where $h$ is pulled back from $\Sigma$. The metric components and lapse $N$ are dimensionless in these length coordinates. This is a static spacetime model: the coefficients are independent of $x^0$, $\partial_{x^0}$ is the selected future timelike Killing field, and $N$ is its lapse, so $g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-N^2$.

The Riemannian volume density of $h$ is denoted by $dV_h$; in length coordinates it has units of cubic metres and finite total volume, and no orientation of $\Sigma$ is required. In a fixed SI gauge, let $\Phi:\Sigma\to\mathbb R$ be a smooth electrostatic scalar potential in volts, let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a fixed charge in coulombs, let $T_0>0$ be a reference temperature in kelvins, and let $\mu_0\in\mathbb R$ be a reference chemical-potential parameter in joules. The sign convention is that the local electrochemical parameter is $\mu_0-q\Phi$. For the static Killing field $\xi=\partial_{x^0}$, its lapse is $N_\xi=N$; fix the Killing-normalized temperature $T_K:=N_\xi T$ to be the constant $T_0$, so the local temperature is $T(x)=T_0/N(x)$. Define the local chemical-potential field by $\mu(x)=(\mu_0-q\Phi(x))/N(x)$ for $x\in\Sigma$; then $q\Phi$ and $\mu$ have units of joules.

Let $D\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ be an open domain for the pair $(T,\mu)$, measured in kelvins and joules, and let $p:D\to\mathbb R$ be a supplied $C^2$ pressure function with values in pascals. Require $(T(x),\mu(x))\in D$ at every $x\in\Sigma$. The function $p$ is model input; this definition does not derive an equation of state or assert that the prescribed data have a material realization.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
